newsitem.title: UK: Good monsoon augurs well for gold demand.
newsitem.headline: Good monsoon augurs well for gold demand.

text.p: A uniformly good Indian monsoon this year augurs well for gold demand in coming months, according to research group Gold Fields Mineral Services (GFMS) chief executive Stewart Murray.
The good rain promises ample harvests to generate income in rural India where gold is bought after the monsoon for dowries and as a primary store of wealth.
"We are moving into the sustained six-month period of Indian demand at its strongest. It augurs well for the future," Murray said, commenting on GFMS's Gold 1996-Update 1, released on Wednesday.
The monsoon had brought adequate rains everywhere with only a few areas where it was excessive for crop development.

"Gold's performance over the medium term will to a large degree be determined by levels of offtake in the physical markets in the months ahead, which represents the seasonally strongest part of the year," he said.

But he said that the direction of the price would depend just as much on levels of producer forward selling, sales from central bank reserves and the perceptions of Western investors about gold's potential as an investment.
Gold hit a six-year London high at $414.80 per ounce on February 5 in a rally led by U.S. investment fund buying but it has languished below $400 in recent weeks.
A combination of official sector sales, private investor dishoarding and lower physical demand combined to restrain then erode gold's price raise, according to GFMS.
GFMS also noted that 108 tonnes of official sector sales during the period was only half of the total from the central banks during the first half of 1995.
"However as further unreported sales may well have taken place during the first half of 1996, the final figure may well be higher than the intial estimate," the report said.

He also noted that the level of disinvestment by European and North American investors during the period was "...the product of disillusionment about gold's prospects of regaining short term...the ground lost after February's price spike".
"In an environment of low U.S. interest rates, many investors have appeared to favour the much more volatile soft commodities and the equities market rather than precious metals," Murray said.
Mine supply rose in the first half after two years of decline due to higher output mainly from Australia and Canada.
A further boost came as higher prices attracted a record level recycling of gold scrap.
GFMS noted that gold demand was significantly lower during the first half of the year compared with first half 1995.

This was largely due to the fall in jewellery fabrication and coin demand and the sharp decline in bar hoarding interest, particularly in Japan where 1995 demand was spurred by the aftermath of banking scandals and the earthquake.
"Demand in the Middle East and India was quite good during the first half while offtake from the Far East and China was weak," said Murray.
Chinese demand was lower due to the government's prolonged austerity programme and the more stable yuan and a growing preference for gem-set jewellery," the GFMS report said.
